content: Patients with hyperparasitemia are at a significantly increased risk of treatment failure, severe malaria, and death. These individuals require close monitoring in addition to receiving artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT). For cases of uncomplicated malaria caused by Plasmodium vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi, if the specific malaria species is not definitively identified, both adults and children should be treated as if they have uncomplicated P. falciparum malaria. This recommendation is strongly supported by high-certainty evidence. In regions where infections are susceptible to chloroquine, adults and children with uncomplicated P. vivax, P. ovale, P. malariae, or P. knowlesi malaria should be treated with either an ACT or chloroquine. However, in areas with chloroquine-resistant infections, treatment with an ACT is recommended. The glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) status of patients should guide the administration of primaquine to prevent relapse in cases of P. vivax or P. ovale malaria. A 14-day course of primaquine is recommended for children and adults in all transmission settings, except for pregnant women, infants under six months of age, breastfeeding women (unless their infants are confirmed not to be G6PD deficient), and individuals with G6PD deficiency. A shorter regimen of 7 days at 0.5 mg/kg/day may improve adherence but carries a higher risk of adverse events and is not recommended. Weekly primaquine at 0.75 mg/kg for 8 weeks can be considered under close medical supervision to prevent relapse. In pregnant or breastfeeding women, weekly chemoprophylaxis with chloroquine can be administered until delivery and breastfeeding are completed. Afterward, primaquine can be given based on G6PD status to prevent future relapses. For severe malaria, adults and children, including infants, pregnant women in all trimesters, and lactating women, should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular artesunate for at least 24 hours or until oral medication can be tolerated. After at least 24 hours of parenteral therapy, treatment should be completed with a 3-day course of an ACT. If artesunate is unavailable, artemether is preferred over quinine for treating severe malaria. In settings where complete treatment for severe malaria is not possible but injections are available, a single intramuscular dose of artesunate should be administered, and the patient should be referred to an appropriate facility. If intramuscular artesunate is unavailable, intramuscular artemether or quinine should be used. For children under six years, a single rectal dose of artesunate (10 mg/kg) can be given before referral, but rectal artesunate is not recommended for older children or adults. National drug and regulatory authorities must ensure that antimalarial medicines provided in both public and private sectors meet acceptable quality standards through regulation, inspection, and enforcement. Malaria programs should regularly monitor the therapeutic efficacy and safety of antimalarial drugs using standard WHO protocols. The choice of ACTs in a country or region should prioritize optimal efficacy, safety, and adherence. Drugs used as first-line treatments should not be used in intermittent preventive treatment (IPTp), post-malaria chemoprevention (PMC), seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), intermittent preventive treatment in schoolchildren (IPTsc), or mass drug administration (MDA). Mass testing and treatment (MTaT) to reduce malaria transmission is not recommended, except in exceptional circumstances, such as in very low transmission or post-elimination settings where MDA is not feasible. Similarly, targeted drug administration (TDA) may be considered in areas with very low transmission or post-elimination settings to prevent re-establishment of transmission. Individuals at increased risk of infection relative to the general population should be prioritized for TDA, provided their infections constitute a significant portion of the parasite reservoir. Routine malaria testing and treatment at points of entry (land, sea, or air) to reduce importation is not recommended due to a lack of evidence and feasibility concerns. However, in areas nearing elimination or post-elimination, organized or identifiable groups arriving from malaria-endemic areas can be tested and treated soon after entry to reduce importation. Reactive case detection and treatment (RACDT) becomes essential in surveillance when countries are nearing malaria elimination or post-elimination to monitor progress and prevent re-establishment of transmission. Reactive indoor residual spraying (IRS) of insecticide can also be conducted in the homes of confirmed cases and neighbors to prevent or reduce malaria transmission in areas approaching elimination or post-elimination. However, the decision to implement reactive IRS should consider the cost, potential benefits, and risk of insecticide resistance.
